newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian investment fund up 15 pct in six weeks.
newsitem.headline: Croatian investment fund up 15 pct in six weeks.

text.p: Croatia's first investment fund, set up by a small private Kaptol Banka, said on Thursday the value of its portfolio had increased 15 percent in six weeks of operating.

The bank was founded a year ago with a 15 million mark ($8.9 million) capital base. It is partly owned and run by Dejan Kosutic, a 26-year old grandson of the powerful Croatian President Franjo Tudjman.
Although one of the latest banks to be licensed in Croatia, it was the first to hit a potentially lucrative market with an open investment fund -- Kaptol Proinvest.
One Proinvest share jumped from 100 kuna on January 8 to 115.1 kuna on February 19, said Snjezana Herceg, director of the bank's investment sector.
The growth was mainly due to a sharp rise of the leading Croatian shares in the first few weeks of the year, she said.
The net profit for investors -- mostly Croatian citizens -- was a little over 10 percent after deducting a five-percent entry commission.
"We started operating just in time to buy cheap some good shares whose price went up almost immediately," Herceg told Reuters.

He said the fund's strategy is relatively conservative, with almost 49 percent of the capital invested in the local money market, up to 40 percent in government bonds and only up to 30 percent in stocks. But there are plans to invest up to 10 percent in real estate in the future.
The fund invests exclusively in Croatia.

"Most of the money is invested in the money market, which is most liquid, so that we can pay off at any time investors who want to quit. That is the limiting factor of having an open fund," Kosutic told Reuters in an interview.
Kaptol Proinvest has so far attracted close to one million kuna and the projection is that it could reach some 20 million by the end of the year, he said.
A Croatian market analyst, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the plan is an "optimistic one", but admitted that breaking the ice has its advantages.

"They were the first, and the only ones so far, to offer this kind of investment and this gives them a potential edge. They could expect their portfolio to expand in the future if things go as anticipated," the analyst said.
The stock market picked up last year after two leading firms -- drug firm Pliva and Zagrebacka Banka -- were listed in London. The turnover at the Zagreb bourse was 70 times up from 1995.
The source said fears that Kosutic could use his family connections to spur business are unfounded.
"That is not a serious danger. He seems to be running the business very professionally and independently. There is no evidence so far that he took advantage of his position," the analyst said.
Kosutic said they were planning other types of funds with a less conservative investment strategy.

Kaptol investments is also positioning itself to take a share in the giant Croatian voucher privatisation scheme, through which the government plans to distribute some 3 billion kuna in shares of leading companies to people most affected by war. ($ = 1.693 German Marks)
